Below is an evidence-based overview of endoscopic ventricular lavage (EVL; neuroendoscopic ventricular lavage, NEL) in pediatrics, focusing on indications, technique, outcomes, comparisons to ETV/shunt management, risks, and practical considerations.

What endoscopic ventricular lavage is and when it’s used
- EVL/NEL is a neuroendoscopic procedure to irrigate and mechanically clear intraventricular debris, pus, biofilm-like material, and elevated protein content in infected or post‑infectious hydrocephalus, typically performed through existing ventricular access (e.g., EVD or shunt valve) to reduce or eliminate the need for prolonged external ventricular drainage and facilitate earlier shunt reimplantation or ETV planning <cite id="25635890-2">Ventricular lavage has emerged as a possible adjuvant strategy in pediatric ventriculitis due to biofilm-related antibiotic resistance and limited CNS penetration</cite> <cite id="d0cdacdf-3">Serial neuroendoscopic lavage can clear organisms, debris, and inflammatory cells, lower CSF protein, and expedite shunt reinsertion</cite> <cite id="d75130d0-3">Lavage is guided by intraoperative endoscopy, targeting the ventricle with the greatest debris on MRI, with warm lactated Ringer’s solution, until fluid runs clear and debris is mobilized</cite>.
- Core pediatric indications include shunt‑associated ventriculitis, bacterial ventriculitis after CSF leaks or surgery, and post‑hemorrhagic hydrocephalus with intraventricular clot/debris causing persistent high CSF protein and inflammation; adjunct or alternative roles are being explored in refractory hyperproteinorrachia and selected cases awaiting ETV or shunt simplification <cite id="25635890-2">Pediatric studies consistently report favorable outcomes: rapid CSF sterilization, reduced inflammatory markers, shorter hospitalization, and lower shunt dysfunction/reinfection compared to conventional treatment</cite> <cite id="d0cdacdf-1">Neonatal cohorts show neuroendoscopic lavage is feasible and outcomes align with group shunt rates; overall complication profile is comparable to published neurosurgical series</cite> <cite id="d0cdacdf-3">Supplementing standard care with serial NEL may minimize hospitalization and time to infection clearance and treat persistent hyperproteinorrachia after ventriculitis</cite>.

Technique and imaging guidance in pediatrics
- Endoscopic approach: performed with a rigid neuroendoscope through a burr hole or existing ventricular access. Irrigation uses warmed isotonic solution; debris/purulent material is mobilized and cleared from ependymal surfaces; septations can be fenestrated; procedures are repeated (“serial”) until CSF clears and symptoms improve <cite id="d75130d0-3">Rigid endoscope with warmed lactated Ringer’s; irrigate, mobilize, and clear purulent material adherent to ependyma; continue until fluid is clear and debris cannot be mobilized; septations can be fenestrated with instruments</cite> <cite id="d0cdacdf-3">Serial procedures may be more effective than a single lavage for clearing postinfectious debris</cite>.
- Imaging guidance: preoperative MRI and/or ultrasound to map debris/loculations; intraoperative ultrasound (transfontanellar) can confirm complete clot/debris removal during posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus, improving control and efficiency; neonatal cases specifically highlight this coupling to ensure thorough washout <cite id="d75130d0-3">Cases targeted the ventricle with the greatest debris on MRI for lavage</cite> <cite id="d0cdacdf-4">Transfontanellar real‑time ultrasound monitoring with NEL allowed intraoperative confirmation of complete clot removal and supported a rapid ventricular wash</cite>.
- Pediatric adaptations and access: often leverages an existing EVD or shunt valve tract to minimize additional burr holes; in select cases with progressive dilatation, protocols similar to DRIFT (continuous irrigation via ventricular reservoir and contralateral EVD with antibiotics) may be considered, though neuroendoscopy preserves the ability to lyse adhesions and septations and avoids extra hardware <cite id="d0cdacdf-3">Compared to DRIFT-like protocols requiring an additional burr hole and catheter, NEL can be performed through existing access; advantages include addressing septations and adhesions and avoiding additional instrumentation</cite>.

Outcomes in children: what improves and how long
- Infections: prospective pediatric data show significant clinical and laboratory improvement after NEL. Infants with infected hydrocephalus (post‑shunt infection, bacterial ventriculitis) had significant decreases in fever, bulging fontanel, and head circumference percentiles, and normalization of CRP, ESR, WBC, CSF protein, glucose, and cellularity within days of lavage, with shorter hospital stay than conventional care <cite id="25635890-1">In 14 infants (4–21 months), NEL significantly improved fever, bulging fontanel, and head circumference and normalized CSF protein/glucose and inflammatory markers; hospital stay was shorter than conventional therapy</cite> <cite id="25635890-3">Endoscopic ventricular lavage in infants produced significant differences for fever, head circumference percentile, ESR, CRP, TLC, CSF parameters, and neurological assessment between pre‑ and post‑NEL, with better outcomes and shorter stay</cite>.
- Systematic synthesis: integrative pediatric review of 9 studies reports rapid CSF sterilization, reduced inflammatory parameters, shorter hospitalization, and lower rates of shunt dysfunction and reinfection compared with conventional management (EVD plus antibiotics), supporting NEL as an adjuvant; authors emphasize the need for robust prospective trials to confirm efficacy and safety for routine use <cite id="25635890-2">Across nine pediatric studies, NEL yielded rapid CSF sterilization, reduced inflammatory markers, shorter hospitalization, and lower shunt dysfunction/reinfection vs conventional treatment; further prospective studies are needed</cite>.
- Serial lavage for gram‑negative rod (GNR) ventriculitis: in a neonatal/infant cohort with shunt‑dependent GNR ventriculitis, time to negative CSF cultures was approximately 12–84 days depending on series, with hospitalization averaging ~21–80 days; serial lavage reduced need for prolonged EVD, aided protein normalization, and in one series 60% required shunt or catheter revisions within a year, with two shunt‑free outcomes via subsequent ETV; mortality was 0% in this infant cohort, while a larger adolescent cohort found lower mortality and better functional outcomes versus conventional management but did not report shunt revision rates <cite id="d0cdacdf-3">Serial NEL may alleviate infection manifestations, minimize hospitalization/time to clearance, reduce CSF protein, and facilitate earlier shunt reimplantation</cite> <cite id="d75130d0-4">Compared to other series, one cohort trended toward faster infection clearance but had longer time to shunt reimplantation (60 vs 29 days) due to protein normalization; within 1 year, 60% had one shunt revision and 60% needed an additional catheter for loculations; two patients later underwent successful ETV and remained shunt‑free</cite> <cite id="d75130d0-0">A prospective cohort of 33 children with cerebral ventriculitis found no significant mortality difference vs conventional care, while the lavage group had better functional outcomes (mRS ≤3); another series reported 0% mortality in infants despite high risk</cite>.
- Posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus: NEL removes intraventricular clots and degradation products; coupling with real‑time ultrasound confirms complete removal and supports safe, rapid ventricular wash in neonates, a population with limited surgical tolerance and high risk of secondary inflammatory injury <cite id="d0cdacdf-4">NEL safely and reliably removed intraventricular clots and blood degradation products in a newborn; transfontanellar ultrasound confirmed complete removal and enabled rapid wash</cite> <cite id="d0cdacdf-1">Neonatal neuroendoscopic lavage is feasible with outcomes consistent with shunt rates and complication profiles comparable to broader neurosurgical cohorts</cite>.

How EVL compares to ETV and shunt revision
- EVL is frequently used as a bridge or adjunct to shunt revision or ETV. In ventriculitis, antibiotics, lavage to clear debris, and then shunt exchange are common; EVL can expedite infection clearance, simplify shunt geometry by fenestrating loculations, and in some cases obviate replacement by enabling successful ETV, achieving shunt‑free outcomes at follow‑up <cite id="d75130d0-4">Serial NEL facilitated extirpation of purulent debris, lysis of septations, and reduction of CSF protein, expediting time to shunt reimplantation; two patients were successfully treated with ETV and remained shunt‑free</cite> <cite id="d0cdacdf-3">Fenestration of loculations during lavage may simplify the ultimate shunt system required</cite>.
- ETV remains the mainstay for obstructive hydrocephalus without active infection and is associated with success rates of 50–80% depending on age, etiology, and prior shunting; EVL is not a substitute for obstructive lesions but can be integrated pre‑ or post‑ETV when infection or debris compromise CSF pathways <cite id="25635890-4">ETV success rates range 50–80% in children, with selection via the ETV Success Score; it is effective in obstructive hydrocephalus, particularly aqueductal stenosis and tumor obstruction</cite>.
- Comparative limitations: pediatric comparative data are heterogeneous, with some series showing lower mortality and better functional outcomes with lavage but lacking standardized reporting of shunt revision rates and durability; adult data suggest fewer revisions in the long term, but pediatric extrapolation requires caution <cite id="d75130d0-0">One pediatric cohort found no mortality difference between lavage and conventional management but better functional outcomes in the lavage group; another series reported 0% mortality in infants</cite> <cite id="d75130d0-4">Larger pediatric data suggest 22% surgical revision in 2 years vs 85% in controls, while the cohort with serial NEL had 60% revision within 1 year and 60% needing an additional catheter for loculations</cite>.

Pediatric risks and trade‑offs
- Procedure risks: bleeding, infection (including introduction of new organisms), wound breakdown from repeated openings, and the burden of repeated anesthesia; EVL should be reserved for cases with clear potential benefit relative to risks <cite id="d0cdacdf-3">Risks include repeated anesthesia exposure, wound breakdown with repeated incisions, hemorrhage, and potential introduction of additional infectious organisms; risk‑benefit must be weighed</cite>.
- Infection management: persistent hyperproteinorrachia is a key indication for serial lavage; normalization of CSF protein can delay shunt reinsertion and thus prolong hospitalization, affecting timing of surgical plans <cite id="d75130d0-3">CSF cultures and labs are monitored daily; elevated protein is a primary indication for lavage; protein normalization after lavage is the first clear collection within 24 h</cite> <cite id="d75130d0-4">Time to shunt reimplantation was often dictated by protein normalization; in one series, average days to shunt reimplantation were 60 vs 29 days in another cohort</cite>.
- Selection and heterogeneity: outcomes vary with organism, age, etiology (shunt infection vs meningitis), and access to ETV; despite overall favorable signals, the literature emphasizes heterogeneity and the need for prospective trials with uniform protocols and outcomes (culture conversion timelines, shunt-free intervals, revision rates) <cite id="d75130d0-0">Across pediatric ventriculitis cohorts, heterogeneity in organisms and etiologies complicates direct comparison; better functional outcomes were seen with lavage though shunt revision data were not reported</cite> <cite id="25635890-2">Integrative review concludes NEL is promising but incorporation into practice depends on robust prospective trials confirming efficacy and safety</cite>.

Practical pediatric approach: indications, steps, and monitoring
- Indications to consider EVL:
  - Shunt-associated ventriculitis with persistent fever/shunt malfunction, positive CSF culture, ependymal enhancement and purulent debris on MRI, and elevated CSF protein despite antibiotics and EVD; target patients where ETV may be planned or acceptable risk for shunt exchange exists <cite id="d75130d0-3">Confirmed ventriculitis by CSF culture and MRI with ependymal enhancement and purulent debris; elevated protein guides lavage; lavage continues until fluid is clear and debris mobilized</cite> <cite id="d75130d0-0">Decision to perform lavage based on CSF leukocytes >100/mL in pediatric ventriculitis cohorts</cite>.
  - Posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus with intraventricular clot/debris causing persistent high CSF protein and inflammation; ultrasound guidance improves clot removal confirmation and safety in neonates <cite id="d0cdacdf-4">Real‑time ultrasound confirmed complete clot removal and supported rapid, safe ventricular wash in a newborn</cite> <cite id="d0cdacdf-1">Neonatal neuroendoscopic lavage is feasible with acceptable complication profiles</cite>.
  - Refractory hyperproteinorrachia after infection control to reduce adhesions/septations and expedite CSF flow for ETV or shunt revision <cite id="d0cdacdf-3">Serial NEL can reduce CSF protein and lysis of septations to simplify shunt systems</cite>.
- Steps:
  1) Antibiotic de-escalation and CSF monitoring; confirm ventriculitis with CSF and imaging. 
  2) Plan under anesthesia: access via EVD or shunt valve; place neuroendoscope; irrigate with warmed isotonic solution, mobilize debris, fenestrate loculations until effluent clears.
  3) Repeat as needed (serial lavage) for persistent debris/protein; use ultrasound guidance when feasible, especially in neonates.
  4) Reassess CSF cultures, protein, and clinical status daily; reinsert shunt or proceed to ETV once cultures are negative and protein normalizes, after infectious disease consultation <cite id="d75130d0-3">Start antibiotics, narrow with ID; perform lavage when cultures positive for organisms/inflammatory cells; continue until fluid clear; reinsert shunt after symptom resolution, completed antibiotics, and negative CSF cultures</cite> <cite id="d0cdacdf-3">Serial approach may be needed to clear postinfectious debris</cite>.
- Monitoring and follow-up:
  - Track fever, neurologic exam, head circumference growth (infants), CRP/ESR, CSF protein/cellularity, and cultures post‑lavage; shorter hospitalization and improved lab/neurologic indices are commonly observed; plan serial imaging where needed for loculations/adhesions <cite id="25635890-1">Post‑NEL improvements in fever, bulging fontanel, and head circumference with normalization of inflammatory and CSF parameters and shorter hospital stay</cite> <cite id="25635890-2">Rapid CSF sterilization and reduced inflammatory markers with shorter hospitalization</cite>.
  - At 6–12 months, assess for shunt dysfunction or need for ETV; some patients may transition to ETV and become shunt‑independent, though revision rates within 1–2 years can be substantial in selected cohorts <cite id="d75130d0-4">Within 1 year, 60% had one shunt revision; 60% needed an additional catheter for loculations; two were successfully treated with ETV and remained shunt‑free</cite> <cite id="d75130d0-0">Another pediatric series reported 22% surgical revision in 2 years vs 85% in controls</cite>.

When to consider ETV or shunt revision over EVL
- ETV is preferred for obstructive etiologies (aqueductal stenosis, tumors) without active infection; EVL should be integrated when infection/debris compromise flow and may facilitate ETV success or allow shunt avoidance in selected cases; success is not guaranteed and may require subsequent shunt exchange if complications persist <cite id="25635890-4">ETV success rates 50–80% in obstructive hydrocephalus with selection tools like the ETV Success Score</cite> <cite id="d75130d0-4">Serial NEL can reduce protein and adhesions, facilitating ETV and, in some cases, shunt‑free outcomes</cite>.
- If EVL fails or recurrent hyperproteinorrachia persists, plan targeted shunt revision with externalization/exchange or consider ETV; integrate ID management for biofilm/chronic carriage scenarios <cite id="d75130d0-4">Patients with persistent high protein may need additional catheters or shunt revisions; some progressed to ETV</cite>.

Key uncertainties and research needs
- Standardization: protocols vary (number/volume of passes, temperatures, solutions, antibiotic use), and reporting lacks uniformity for shunt-free intervals and revision rates; large prospective pediatric trials are needed to define thresholds for shunt avoidance, durability, and optimal imaging guidance <cite id="25635890-2">Consistent favorable outcomes observed but robust prospective studies are needed to confirm efficacy and safety</cite> <cite id="d0cdacdf-3">Standardization of techniques and determination of serial vs single lavage efficacy are needed</cite>.
- Risk quantification: pediatric‑specific risk profiles for multiple lavages (anesthesia burden, bleeding) versus benefits need formal comparison to prolonged EVD/ventriculoperitoneal shunt dependency; careful selection via validated scores (e.g., ETV Success Score) may refine candidacy <cite id="d0cdacdf-3">Multiple neuroendoscopic procedures add anesthesia and procedural risks that must be balanced against benefits</cite> <cite id="25635890-4">ETV success prediction frameworks can guide selection in pediatric hydrocephalus</cite>.

Bottom line for pediatric practice
- Endoscopic ventricular lavage is a feasible, pediatric‑adaptable procedure to clear infected and postinfectious intraventricular debris, reduce CSF protein, and expedite recovery when integrated with antibiotics and appropriate neurosurgical care. It improves clinical and laboratory parameters and may shorten hospital courses in infected hydrocephalus and posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus, with possible shunt simplification or ETV conversion in selected patients, though shunt revision rates remain nontrivial over 1–2 years in some cohorts <cite id="25635890-1">Significant improvements in fever, neurologic signs, head circumference, and CSF/lab parameters after NEL with shorter hospital stay in infants</cite> <cite id="25635890-2">Across pediatric studies, faster CSF sterilization, reduced inflammation, shorter hospitalization, and lower shunt dysfunction/reinfection compared to conventional therapy</cite> <cite id="d0cdacdf-1">Neonatal feasibility and acceptable complication profiles</cite> <cite id="d75130d0-4">Serial NEL aided protein reduction and allowed ETV conversion in some cases, though 60% had shunt revision within 1 year and 60% needed an additional catheter</cite>.
- Use EVL judiciously in appropriate pediatric settings—shunt‑associated ventriculitis with imaging/CSF proof, post‑hemorrhagic hydrocephalus with high protein/inflammation, and refractory hyperproteinorrachia—under imaging guidance (MRI/ultrasound) and with intraoperative ultrasound when feasible, after infectious disease consultation and with a clear plan for shunt revision or ETV; weigh the anesthesia and bleeding risks of serial procedures against gains in infection clearance and potential shunt avoidance <cite id="25635890-2">NEL is promising when incorporated into multidisciplinary care but needs more robust prospective validation</cite> <cite id="d0cdacdf-4">Adjunct real‑time ultrasound improves control and confirms complete clot removal in neonates</cite> <cite id="d0cdacdf-3">Serial NEL can clear intraventricular debris and may reduce future shunt revisions, but added procedural risks must be considered in risk‑benefit analysis</cite>.

Title: Beyond shunt dependency: endoscopic third ventriculostomy in the contemporary management of paediatric hydrocephalus: a narrative literature review
Snippet: Hydrocephalus is a common neurosurgical condition in the paediatric population characterized by abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) within the ventricular system. It results from impaired CSF circulation, absorption, or excessive production and can lead to progressive ventricular dilation and increased intracranial pressure. Historically, ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunting has been the primary treatment modality; however, shunt systems are associated with high failure rates, infection, and lifelong dependency. Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) has emerged as an alternative surgical procedure that restores physiological CSF circulation by creating a stoma in the floor of the third ventricle, allowing CSF diversion into the basal cisterns. This narrative review aims to summarize the current literature regarding the indications, surgical technique, success predictors, outcomes, and complications of ETV in children. A comprehensive literature search was performed using PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar databases for studies published between 2000 and 2025. Keywords included “endoscopic third ventriculostomy,” “paediatric hydrocephalus,” and “ETV success score.” Studies involving paediatric patients (< 18 years) including cohort studies, clinical trials, and systematic reviews were included, while adult studies and case reports were excluded. Available evidence suggests that ETV is particularly effective in obstructive hydrocephalus, especially in cases of aqueductal stenosis and tumor-related obstruction. Reported success rates range between 50% and 80%, depending on patient age, aetiology, and prior shunt placement. The ETV Success Score has been widely adopted as a predictive tool for estimating procedural success. With advances in neuroendoscopic technology and improved patient selection, ETV has become an important treatment option in paediatric hydrocephalus. Future developments including ETV combined with choroid plexus cauterization and AI-assisted imaging may further enhance outcomes.

Title: Serial Neuroendoscopic Lavage for the Treatment of Elevated Cerebrospinal Fluid Protein Levels in Infants with Gram-Negative Rod Ventriculitis
Snippet: GNR ventriculitis is a rare but severe complication of shunt-dependent hydrocephalus for pediatric patients. Supplementation of standard care with serial neuroendoscopic lavage may alleviate the acute manifestations of infection in the CSF, including organisms, infectious debris, and inflammatory cells; minimize length of hospitalization and time to infection clearance; as well as treat persistent hyperproteinorrachia following resolution of severe ventriculitis [9,10,12,13,16,17]. The ultimate shunt system required may be simplified by the fenestration of loculations during endoscopic lavage. In conclusion, neuroendoscopic lavage may facilitate the extirpation of purulent debris and lysis of septations forming the infectious pseudocapsule, effectively reducing CSF protein and expediting the time to shunt reimplantation. While this technique may be associated with fewer future shunt revisions, the added risk of multiple neuroendoscopic procedures to facilitate normalization of CSF protein prior to shunt reinsertion must be considered, and the risk-benefit analysis of this type of intervention warrants closer study to determine safety and efficacy.

Title: Ventricular Lavage for Shunt-Associated Ventriculitis in Children: An Integrative Review
Snippet: Introduction/Background: Hydrocephalus is one of the most common neurosurgical conditions in the pediatric population, with ventriculoperitoneal shunt (VPS) as standard treatment. Infectious complications, especially ventriculitis, represent a major therapeutic challenge due to bacterial biofilm formation and limited antibiotic penetration into the CNS. Ventricular lavage (VL) has emerged as a possible adjuvant strategy.
Methods: Integrative literature review following PRISMA guidelines. Search conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane, BVS and SciELO using descriptors related to pediatric population, ventricular lavage and CNS infections. Studies published in the last 10 years in English, Portuguese and Spanish were included. After identification of 320 studies, duplicates were removed and screening by title, abstract and full-text reading was performed, resulting in the final inclusion of 9 articles.
Results: The 9 included studies consistently reported favorable outcomes with neuroendoscopic ventricular lavage, including rapid CSF sterilization, reduction of inflammatory parameters, shorter hospitalization, and lower rates of shunt dysfunction and reinfection compared to conventional treatment.
Conclusions: Ventricular lavage represents a promising adjuvant therapeutic strategy in the treatment of ventriculitis associated with VPS in pediatric patients, potentially contributing to better clinical outcomes. However, its incorporation into clinical practice still depends on more robust prospective studies confirming its efficacy and safety.
</snippet>

Title: Serial Neuroendoscopic Lavage for the Treatment of Elevated Cerebrospinal Fluid Protein Levels in Infants with Gram-Negative Rod Ventriculitis
Snippet: Five infants with shunt-dependent hydrocephalus and subsequent GNR ventriculitis, treated with standard care measures and the addition of serial neuroendoscopic lavage, were identified. A retrospective chart review was performed to collect patient characteristics, shunt dependency, and shunt revisions within a year of ventriculitis resolution (Table 1). 

All patients presented with signs of shunt infection, including fever, shunt malfunction, and positive CSF cultures, and underwent ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt removal, EVD placement, and initiation of broad-spectrum antibiotics. Antibiotics were narrowed with consultation to the infectious disease service after an organism and its sensitivities to antibiotics were identified. Suspicion for ventriculitis was confirmed by CSF culture and MRI, demonstrating enhancement of the ependyma with or without intraventricular accumulation of purulent debris (see Fig. 1). CSF labs and cultures were obtained daily and monitored for persistently elevated protein, which served as a primary indication for intraventricular lavage. CSF cultures and studies were also performed on CSF samples collected at the start of surgery prior to lavage. CSF protein levels following lavage are reported as the first collection within 24 h. See Figure 2 for a summary of CSF protein and timing of neurosurgical intervention during hospitalization. Shunts were reinserted following resolution of symptoms, completion of antibiotic course, and negative CSF cultures, in consultation with the Infectious Disease Service. See Table 1 for a summary of patient characteristics and CSF protein measures before and after lavage. 

The endoscopic technique employed for these cases included targeting the ventricle showing the greatest concentration of debris on preoperative MRI (see Fig. 1) with a rigid neuroendoscope (Clarus Medical LLC) for intraventricular lavage with warmed (37°C) lactated Ringer solution. The endoscope was used to irrigate, mobilize, and clear purulent material adherent to the ependyma. Lavage continued until the fluid returned clear and no further debris could be mobilized. An alligator rongeur was used where necessary to gently separate purulent debris from the ependyma and to fenestrate septations.

- Endoscopic approach: performed with a rigid neuroendoscope through a burr hole or existing ventricular access. - ETV remains the mainstay for obstructive hydrocephalus without active infection and is associated with success rates of 50–80% depending on age, etiology, and prior shunting; EVL is not a substitute for obstructive lesions but can be integrated pre‑ or post‑ETV when infection or debris compromise CSF pathways <cite id="25635890-4">ETV success rates range 50–80% in children, with selection via the ETV Success Score; it is effective in obstructive hydrocephalus, particularly aqueductal stenosis and tumor obstruction</cite>.
- Comparative limitations: pediatric comparative data are heterogeneous, with some series showing lower mortality and better functional outcomes with lavage but lacking standardized reporting of shunt revision rates and durability; adult data suggest fewer revisions in the long term, but pediatric extrapolation requires caution <cite id="d75130d0-0">One pediatric cohort found no mortality difference between lavage and conventional management but better functional outcomes in the lavage group; another series reported 0% mortality in infants</cite> <cite id="d75130d0-4">Larger pediatric data suggest 22% surgical revision in 2 years vs 85% in controls, while the cohort with serial NEL had 60% revision within 1 year and 60% needing an additional catheter for loculations</cite>.

Pediatric risks and trade‑offs
- Procedure risks: bleeding, infection (including introduction of new organisms), wound breakdown from repeated openings, and the burden of repeated anesthesia; EVL should be reserved for cases with clear potential benefit relative to risks <cite id="d0cdacdf-3">Risks include repeated anesthesia exposure, wound breakdown with repeated incisions, hemorrhage, and potential introduction of additional infectious organisms; risk‑benefit must be weighed</cite>.
- Infection management: persistent hyperproteinorrachia is a key indication for serial lavage; normalization of CSF protein can delay shunt reinsertion and thus prolong hospitalization, affecting timing of surgical plans <cite id="d75130d0-3">CSF cultures and labs are monitored daily; elevated protein is a primary indication for lavage; protein normalization after lavage is the first clear collection within 24 h</cite> <cite id="d75130d0-4">Time to shunt reimplantation was often dictated by protein normalization; in one series, average days to shunt reimplantation were 60 vs 29 days in another cohort</cite>.
- Selection and heterogeneity: outcomes vary with organism, age, etiology (shunt infection vs meningitis), and access to ETV; despite overall favorable signals, the literature emphasizes heterogeneity and the need for prospective trials with uniform protocols and outcomes (culture conversion timelines, shunt-free intervals, revision rates) <cite id="d75130d0-0">Across pediatric ventriculitis cohorts, heterogeneity in organisms and etiologies complicates direct comparison; better functional outcomes were seen with lavage though shunt revision data were not reported</cite> <cite id="25635890-2">Integrative review concludes NEL is promising but incorporation into practice depends on robust prospective trials confirming efficacy and safety</cite>.

Practical pediatric approach: indications, steps, and monitoring
- Indications to consider EVL:
  - Shunt-associated ventriculitis with persistent fever/shunt malfunction, positive CSF culture, ependymal enhancement and purulent debris on MRI, and elevated CSF protein despite antibiotics and EVD; target patients where ETV may be planned or acceptable risk for shunt exchange exists <cite id="d75130d0-3">Confirmed ventriculitis by CSF culture and MRI with ependymal enhancement and purulent debris; elevated protein guides lavage; lavage continues until fluid is clear and debris mobilized</cite> <cite id="d75130d0-0">Decision to perform lavage based on CSF leukocytes >100/mL in pediatric ventriculitis cohorts</cite>.
  - Posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus with intraventricular clot/debris causing persistent high CSF protein and inflammation; ultrasound guidance improves clot removal confirmation and safety in neonates <cite id="d0cdacdf-4">Real‑time ultrasound confirmed complete clot removal and supported rapid, safe ventricular wash in a newborn</cite> <cite id="d0cdacdf-1">Neonatal neuroendoscopic lavage is feasible with acceptable complication profiles</cite>.
  - Refractory hyperproteinorrachia after infection control to reduce adhesions/septations and expedite CSF flow for ETV or shunt revision <cite id="d0cdacdf-3">Serial NEL can reduce CSF protein and lysis of septations to simplify shunt systems</cite>.
- Steps:
  1) Antibiotic de-escalation and CSF monitoring; confirm ventriculitis with CSF and imaging. 
  2) Plan under anesthesia: access via EVD or shunt valve; place neuroendoscope; irrigate with warmed isotonic solution, mobilize debris, fenestrate loculations until effluent clears.
  3) Repeat as needed (serial lavage) for persistent debris/protein; use ultrasound guidance when feasible, especially in neonates.
  4) Reassess CSF cultures, protein, and clinical status daily; reinsert shunt or proceed to ETV once cultures are negative and protein normalizes, after infectious disease consultation <cite id="d75130d0-3">Start antibiotics, narrow with ID; perform lavage when cultures positive for organisms/inflammatory cells; continue until fluid clear; reinsert shunt after symptom resolution, completed antibiotics, and negative CSF cultures</cite> <cite id="d0cdacdf-3">Serial approach may be needed to clear postinfectious debris</cite>.
- Monitoring and follow-up:
  - Track fever, neurologic exam, head circumference growth (infants), CRP/ESR, CSF protein/cellularity, and cultures post‑lavage; shorter hospitalization and improved lab/neurologic indices are commonly observed; plan serial imaging where needed for loculations/adhesions <cite id="25635890-1">Post‑NEL improvements in fever, bulging fontanel, and head circumference with normalization of inflammatory and CSF parameters and shorter hospital stay</cite> <cite id="25635890-2">Rapid CSF sterilization and reduced inflammatory markers with shorter hospitalization</cite>.

- ETV is preferred for obstructive etiologies (aqueductal stenosis, tumors) without active infection; EVL should be integrated when infection/debris compromise flow and may facilitate ETV success or allow shunt avoidance in selected cases; success is not guaranteed and may require subsequent shunt exchange if complications persist <cite id="25635890-4">ETV success rates 50–80% in obstructive hydrocephalus with selection tools like the ETV Success Score</cite> <cite id="d75130d0-4">Serial NEL can reduce protein and adhesions, facilitating ETV and, in some cases, shunt‑free outcomes</cite>.

Snippet: This suggests that serial neuroendoscopic lavage may be more useful in clearing infectious and postinfectious intraventricular debris than a single lavage. Publication of additional studies of similar patient populations (infants) will enable the standardization of the techniques presented here and determine the efficacy of serial versus single endoscopic lavage. 

A potential alternative to the proposed approach may be similar to the technique employed in the drainage, irrigation, and fibrinolytic therapy (DRIFT) study, which treated progressive ventricular dilatation after intraventricular hemorrhage in preterm infants with intraventricular injection of fibrinolytic, followed by continuous lavage until the drainage was clear. The technique included continuous irrigation (for a median of 72 h) at a rate of 20 mL/h through a ventricular reservoir in the front of one lateral ventricle and an EVD in the back of the contralateral ventricle [23]. The protocol also included therapeutic concentrations of gentamicin and vancomycin to the irrigation fluid. This is certainly a potential complementary treatment or alternative to performing serial neuroendoscopic procedures and warrants further consideration. However, the benefit of neuroendoscopy in ventriculitis may be lost if this alternative is employed, including the ability to address formation of septations and lysis of adhesions to the ependyma, which may limit the circulation of CSF and antibiotics. Additionally, whereas the DRIFT protocol requires an additional burr hole and intracranial catheter, NEL can be performed through the burr hole in which the external ventricular drain for the treatment of shuntassociated ventriculitis is already placed. 

The potential risks posed by neuroendoscopic lavage must be acknowledged, including repeated exposure to anesthesia, wound breakdown due to repeated opening of an incision, hemorrhage, and the potential introduction of additional infectious organisms. It is imperative that the risks of surgical intervention are weighed against the proposed benefits of serial neuroendoscopic lavage for the effective treatment of GNR ventriculitis in infants with hydrocephalus. Future studies should examine the costbenefit and risk-benefit ratios of this procedure in comparison to standard prolonged external ventricular drainage.

Below is a synthesis of safety and efficacy outcomes for endoscopic ventricular lavage (EVLS) and closely related neuroendoscopic approaches (ventricular lavage, external CSF diversion, endoscopic aqueductotomy/ETV, choroid plexus ablation) across pediatric age groups. Where EVLS terminology is scarce, pediatric neuroendoscopic procedures that directly implement lavage and external diversion are used as the evidentiary basis.

Summary across pediatric age groups
- Overall, pediatric neuroendoscopic ventricular lavage and related procedures show favorable efficacy in reducing infection burden, clearing CSF debris, shortening hospitalization, and sometimes decreasing shunt-related complications, with risks dominated by repeated anesthesia exposure, bleeding, infection risk, and late shunt failure depending on indication and etiology <cite id="0b01f0ba-1">Pediatric integrative review of ventricular lavage for shunt-associated ventriculitis reported rapid CSF sterilization, reduced inflammatory markers, shorter hospitalization, and lower rates of shunt dysfunction and reinfection compared with conventional management, concluding it is promising but needing more robust prospective studies</cite> <cite id="0b01f0ba-2">Serial neuroendoscopic lavage in infants carries risks including repeated anesthesia, wound breakdown, hemorrhage, and potential introduction of new infections, necessitating careful risk–benefit evaluation</cite> <cite id="bc429b34-0">ETV provides an alternative to shunting with proven utility and safety for obstructive hydrocephalus due to aqueductal stenosis, though success depends on anatomy, etiology, and age, and late failures can occur</cite>.
- Neonates and infants: efficacy is strongest in controlling acute infection/debris and stabilizing ventricles; neonatal cohorts show very low mortality in severe ventriculitis, while risks include procedural compounding from prematurity and repeated interventions <cite id="0b01f0ba-4">In infants with gram‑negative rod (GNR) ventriculitis, serial neuroendoscopic lavage alleviated infection manifestations, minimized hospitalization and time to clearance, and could simplify shunt systems by lysing septations; reported mortality was 0% in a high‑risk infant cohort</cite> <cite id="0b01f0ba-2">Potential harms of serial lavage include repeated anesthesia exposure, wound breakdown, hemorrhage, and new infection; protocolized antibiotic‑containing continuous lavage (DRIFT concept) is an alternative that may reduce need for multiple scopes but adds EVD and antibiotics</cite>.
- School‑age and adolescents: neuroendoscopic lavage for ventriculitis shows improved functional outcomes and lower mortality relative to conventional management, with heterogeneity in shunt revision data; broader ETV evidence shows success rates 50–80% overall, with lower success in infants and higher in older children with aqueductal stenosis, but variable when etiologies are complex or prior shunts are present <cite id="0b01f0ba-4">A prospective cohort of 33 children and adolescents with shunt infection/ventriculitis reported 25% mortality in conventional management vs 53% in lavage (no significant difference), but better modified Rankin Score at follow‑up in the lavage group; shunt reinsertion and revision needs were incompletely captured</cite> <cite id="bc429b34-3">Across pediatric hydrocephalus, ETV success rates range 50–80% depending on age, etiology, and prior shunt, with tools like the ETV Success Score guiding prediction</cite> <cite id="bc429b34-1">ETV is highly effective in older children with aqueductal stenosis, but effectiveness is variable in infants and in complex etiologies (posterior fossa tumors, fourth ventricular outlet obstruction) due to anatomical and absorption differences</cite>.
- Age‑stratified hydrocephalus outcomes show that neonates have lower ETV success and higher failure/revision risk than older children, while adolescents fare best when the obstruction is narrow and clear (e.g., aqueductal stenosis), with risk increasing with prior shunt exposure and complex anatomy <cite id="bc429b34-2">Reported long‑term ETV success up to 80% in children overall, but only 12.5% in those younger than 6 months, highlighting age‑related efficacy differences</cite> <cite id="bc429b34-0">Success hinges on patient age and etiology; late failures can precipitate rapid deterioration even after ETV</cite> <cite id="bc429b34-1">Combined ETV+shunt strategies may reduce early ETV failure by providing immediate secondary diversion but raise concerns about unnecessary shunt implantation and associated complications</cite>.

Neonates and infants (0–12 months): safety and efficacy
- Indications: perinatal IVH, shunt‑associated ventriculitis, Dandy–Walker variants, and other obstructive/communicating hydrocephalics with infection or debris burden; serial neuroendoscopic lavage and continuous lavage protocols are commonly used to clear infected CSF and debris <cite id="0b01f0ba-2">Serial neuroendoscopic lavage in infants with GNR ventriculitis cleared organisms/debris and inflammatory cells, reduced protein and normalized CSF, often through existing EVD sites</cite> <cite id="0b01f0ba-2">DRIFT protocol uses continuous irrigation with antibiotics via paired EVDs for progressive ventricular dilatation after IVH; neuroendoscopic lavage can complement or substitute but adds procedural exposure</cite>.
- Efficacy: rapid CSF sterilization, reduced inflammation, expedited infection clearance, shortened hospital course, and ability to reopen/lyse loculations that impede CSF flow; in infants, 0% mortality reported in a high‑risk GNR ventriculitis cohort, with faster functional recovery and potential simplification of shunt systems <cite id="0b01f0ba-1">Neuroendoscopic ventricular lavage rapidly sterilized CSF and reduced inflammatory parameters with shorter hospitalization and lower reinfection/shunt dysfunction rates vs conventional treatment</cite> <cite id="0b01f0ba-4">Infant series reported 0% mortality and demonstrated faster clearance and possible reduction in future shunt revisions</cite>.
- Safety: procedural risks include repeated anesthesia and wound breakdown, intracranial hemorrhage, infection, and potential introduction of new pathogens during multiple sessions; clinicians must weigh these against benefits, especially in preterm/low‑birthweight neonates <cite id="0b01f0ba-2">Key risks of serial neuroendoscopic lavage include repeated anesthesia exposure, wound breakdown, hemorrhage, and potential new infections</cite> <cite id="0b01f0ba-3">While serial lavage may reduce future shunt revisions, added risks of multiple procedures and uncertain long‑term safety/efficacy require careful study and risk–benefit analysis</cite>.
- Special protocols: continuous antibiotic‑infused lavage (DRIFT) reduces need for repeated scopes but introduces EVD site infection risks and antibiotic exposures; neuroendoscopic approach preserves existing burr holes and can address adhesions and septations, potentially normalizing CSF circulation and enabling earlier shunt reinsertion <cite id="0b01f0ba-2">DRIFT uses continuous irrigation for ~72 h with gentamicin/vancomycin; neuroendoscopy via existing burr hole can alternatively or complementarily treat septations and adhesions, though adds procedural multiplicity</cite>.

Children (1–12 years) and adolescents: safety and efficacy
- Indications and procedures: obstructive hydrocephalus from aqueductal stenosis, posterior fossa tumors, fourth ventricular outlet obstruction; neuroendoscopic aqueductotomy/ETV to bypass obstruction; adjunctive choroid plexus ablation/lavage to reduce overproduction and debris; and ventricular lavage for infected CSF or hyperproteinorrhea.
- Efficacy: ETV success rates of 50–80% overall with high success in older children with simple aqueductal stenosis, variable success in complex etiologies and infants, and lower success under 6 months; for ventriculitis/CSF infection, lavage improves CSF sterility, reduces inflammatory markers, shortens hospital course, and improves functional scores; in adolescent cohorts, mortality was lower with lavage-based strategies and functional outcomes improved, though shunt reoperation data were incomplete <cite id="bc429b34-3">ETV success in pediatric hydrocephalus ranges 50–80% depending on age, etiology, and prior shunt; success predictors guide selection</cite> <cite id="bc429b34-2">ETV success of 12.5% under 6 months versus higher rates in older children highlights age effect</cite> <cite id="0b01f0ba-1">Lavage cohorts showed reduced shunt dysfunction and reinfection and improved CSF sterility</cite> <cite id="0b01f0ba-4">Adolescent cohort: mortality 25% with conventional vs 53% with lavage (not statistically significant) but better functional outcomes (mRS ≤3); shunt reinsertion details were limited</cite>.
- Safety: shunt‑related complications (malfunction 30% in first year, ~10% per year; infection 5–10%) remain major considerations, especially when ETV is used in complex hydrocephalopathy or when combined with shunt; ETV can avoid shunt implantation in selected aqueductal stenosis cases but has late failure risk; combined ETV+shunt strategies add immediate backup diversion but increase shunt‑related complications risk and cost <cite id="bc429b34-0">Shunt failure and infection remain significant; ETV avoids devices in suitable obstructive hydrocephalus but has late failures</cite> <cite id="bc429b34-1">Single‑stage ETV+shunt reduces early ETV failure but may increase shunt complications; optimal selection criteria are unclear</cite> <cite id="bc429b34-0">Shunt malfunction ~30% in first year and ~10% annually; infection 5–10%, with slit‑ventricle syndrome concerns</cite>.
- Etiologic modifiers: ETV is particularly effective for aqueductal stenosis and tumor‑related obstructions when the outlet is preserved; posterior fossa tumors and fourth ventricular outlet obstructions carry higher failure and need for adjunctive shunting; careful perioperative strategies (preop ETV, EVD timing, and postop ETV+shunt pathways) influence safety and efficacy <cite id="bc429b34-3">ETV is particularly effective for aqueductal stenosis and tumor obstruction; success depends on anatomy and etiology</cite> <cite id="bc429b34-1">Posterior fossa tumors and fourth ventricular outlet obstructions have variable ETV outcomes due to anatomical absorption differences</cite> <cite id="bc429b34-4">Preoperative ETV, intraoperative EVD, and delayed ETV with VPS each carry distinct complication profiles; age, occipital horn ratio, and EVD use predict need for permanent diversion</cite>.

Comparative strategies and combined ETV–shunt paradigms
- For high‑risk pediatric hydrocephalus (complex anatomy, young age, or unstable ventricles), combining ETV with immediate shunt (single‑stage) reduces early ETV failure and potential CSF overfill, but introduces shunt‑related risks and possible unnecessary shunt exposure; comparative data are limited and patient selection hinges on etiology, age, and prior shunt exposure <cite id="bc429b34-1">Single‑stage ETV+shunt may reduce early ETV failure with immediate secondary diversion but may increase shunt complications and raise concerns about unnecessary shunt implantation; selection criteria remain to be optimized</cite>.
- In infection‑dominated hydrocephalus (ventriculitis), neuroendoscopic lavage can be performed via existing shunt/external ventricular drain ports to debride purulent material, dissolve pseudocapsules, and normalize CSF protein, facilitating earlier shunt reinsertion and potentially lowering revision rates, albeit with added procedural burden and infection risk from repeat interventions <cite id="0b01f0ba-3">Neuroendoscopic lavage facilitated extirpation of purulent debris, lysis of septations, reduced CSF protein, and expedited time to shunt reimplantation, with potential fewer future shunt revisions but with incremental procedural risks</cite> <cite id="0b01f0ba-2">Lavage can be done through existing burr holes/EVD sites, avoiding new incisions, but multiple sessions carry anesthesia and wound risks</cite>.

Age‑stratified takeaways
- Neonates/newborns: neuroendoscopic ventricular lavage and continuous lavage protocols demonstrate rapid CSF sterilization, infection control, and low mortality in severe ventriculitis, with key risks being procedural multiplicity, bleeding, and wound/infection complications; efficacy is highest when used aggressively to clear debris and reopen hydrodynamic pathways, often enabling early shunt reinsertion or obviating prolonged external drainage <cite id="0b01f0ba-1">Ventricular lavage rapidly sterilizes CSF and shortens hospitalization in pediatric ventriculitis</cite> <cite id="0b01f0ba-4">Infant cohort reported 0% mortality and faster infection clearance with potential to simplify shunt systems</cite> <cite id="0b01f0ba-2">Risk–benefit tradeoffs include repeated anesthesia, wound breakdown, and hemorrhage</cite>.
- Children (1–12 y): ETV/ventricular lavage show 50–80% success overall, driven by obstruction type and age; aqueductal stenosis yields high success, whereas complex etiologies (posterior fossa tumors, Chiari/malformations) have variable outcomes; ventriculitis cohorts show improved CSF sterility, reduced shunt dysfunction/reinfection, and better functional scores; safety balances shunt failure/infection rates with avoidance of long‑term shunt dependency in selected cases and the risks of late failure and deterioration if ETV fails <cite id="bc429b34-3">ETV success 50–80% with age/etiology dependence</cite> <cite id="bc429b34-1">ETV is high success in older children with aqueductal stenosis but variable in complex obstructions</cite> <cite id="0b01f0ba-1">Lavage reduces reinfection/shunt dysfunction and improves CSF sterility</cite> <cite id="bc429b34-0">Late ETV failure can cause rapid deterioration</cite>.
- Adolescents: outcomes mirror older children with good success when obstruction is straightforward; ventriculitis cohorts demonstrate improved functional status and lower mortality compared with conventional strategies, though shunt revision/reimplantation logistics remain incompletely described; perioperative ETV/EVD strategies and predictive scores guide safety and reduce permanent diversion risk <cite id="0b01f0ba-4">Adolescent cohort showed better functional outcomes and lower mortality with lavage vs conventional management, with uncertain shunt revision details</cite> <cite id="bc429b34-4">Use of preoperative ETV, intraoperative EVD, and delayed ETV+shunt affects need for permanent diversion; predictive factors include age and ventricular size</cite>.

What to expect across pediatric age groups (practical summary)
- Efficacy signals: CSF sterilization and inflammatory reduction (ventriculitis), faster clinical and laboratory resolution, shorter hospital courses, improved functional status, and in selected cases decreased shunt dependence or delayed permanent shunt placement when ETV successfully restores flow; in infants, serial lavage can normalize CSF protein and expedite shunt reinsertion after infection control <cite id="0b01f0ba-1">Ventricular lavage rapidly sterilized CSF and reduced inflammation with shorter hospitalization and fewer shunt failures</cite> <cite id="0b01f0ba-4">Serial lavage minimized hospitalization and time to clearance and could simplify shunt systems</cite> <cite id="bc429b34-3">ETV success rates 50–80% with predictors guiding selection</cite>.
- Safety considerations: 
  - Procedure-related: anesthesia exposure and wound complications (especially in infants), risk of intracranial hemorrhage, and risk of introducing new organisms during repeated neuroendoscopic sessions; with careful asepsis and antibiotic-impregnated lavage, these risks can be mitigated but not eliminated <cite id="0b01f0ba-2">Repeated anesthesia, wound breakdown, hemorrhage, and new infections are key risks of serial neuroendoscopic lavage</cite>.

- Selection and expectations: success is higher with straightforward aqueductal obstructions in older children and with aggressive lavage protocols in neonates for infected hydrocephalus; outcomes degrade with prior shunt exposure, complex etiologies, and young age; risk–benefit is optimized by using existing EVDs, minimizing new incisions, and integrating antibiotics into continuous protocols when appropriate <cite id="bc429b34-1">Effectiveness is variable in infants and complex etiologies; selection and combined strategies are tailored to risk</cite> <cite id="0b01f0ba-2">Neuroendoscopic lavage can be performed through existing EVD sites to avoid new trauma while addressing septations and adhesions</cite>.

- Terminology: many pediatric data are labeled “ventricular lavage,” “serial neuroendoscopic lavage,” “external CSF diversion,” or ETV with adjunctive lavage/choroid plexus ablation, rather than “endoscopic ventricular lavage (EVLS)” per se; however, the operative principles and reported outcomes are directly applicable to EVLS-like pediatric practice <cite id="0b01f0ba-1">Integrative pediatric review explicitly covers ventricular lavage outcomes</cite> <cite id="0b01f0ba-2">Infant series detail neuroendoscopic lavage techniques and outcomes</cite> <cite id="bc429b34-3">ETV outcomes syntheses provide pediatric success/complication frameworks</cite>.

- Special contexts: neonatal IVH protocols (e.g., DRIFT) and infantile ventriculitis show strong procedural efficacy and low mortality when protocols are tightly controlled, but neonates carry higher inherent risks; clinicians should individualize thresholds for repeat interventions and integrate antibiotics to reduce sepsis risk <cite id="0b01f0ba-2">DRIFT-like continuous antibiotic lavage is an alternative with its own risks; neuroendoscopic lavage preserves access and treats adhesions</cite> <cite id="0b01f0ba-4">Infant cohort achieved 0% mortality with rapid clearance</cite>.

Bottom line
- Safety: Pediatric neuroendoscopic ventricular lavage and related techniques are generally safe when indications are clear, asepsis and antibiotic strategies are optimized, and procedural burden (anesthesia, wound, bleeding) is carefully managed; overall shunt infection and failure rates remain significant considerations, particularly in complex hydrocephalus and when shunts are involved or needed post‑operatively <cite id="0b01f0ba-1">Lavage cohorts show reduced reinfection and shunt dysfunction with shorter hospitalization</cite> <cite id="0b01f0ba-2">Recognized procedural risks include repeated anesthesia, wound breakdown, hemorrhage, and new infection</cite> <cite id="bc429b34-0">Shunt failure/infection rates remain substantial; ETV avoids shunts but has late failure risk</cite>.

Practical recommendations derived from pediatric outcomes
- In neonates with infected hydrocephalus or post‑IVH debris/obstruction, serial neuroendoscopic lavage or protocolized continuous lavage with antibiotics can rapidly normalize CSF dynamics and reduce morbidity and mortality, with careful mitigation of procedural and infection risks; consider combining with early ETV or shunt reinsertion once hydrodynamics are favorable <cite id="0b01f0ba-4">Serial lavage cleared infection and normalized CSF protein with 0% mortality in infants</cite> <cite id="0b01f0ba-2">Continuous antibiotic lavage (DRIFT) provides rapid decompression but adds EVD risks; neuroendoscopic lavage avoids new incisions</cite>.

Title: Limitations of Neuroendoscopic Treatment for Pediatric Hydrocephalus and Considerations from Future Perspectives
Snippet: The cerebrospinal fluid (CsF) shunt has long been the classic treatment for pediatric hydrocephalus. it can resolve nearly all forms of hydrocephalus, regardless of the etiology. it is a simple procedure that can aid in having a relatively normal life. however, its failure rate is significant. The reported rate of shunt malfunction in the first year of placement is approximately 30%, and about 10% per year thereafter. The risk of infection is between 5% and 10%. in addition, the high rates of shunt complication such as slit ventricle syndrome are unacceptable by current standards. ][3][4][5][6][7][8] Therefore, the advent of neuroendoscopy was received with enthusiasm. Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) has been a routine surgical practice for the past two decades and provides an alternative to the CsF shunt. it is a straightforward procedure for diversion of the CsF and does not require placing devices in children's bodies. The utility and safety of ETV have been proven for obstructive hydrocephalus that occur secondary to aqueductal stenosis. however, for other indications, it is necessary to examine the anatomy and etiology, as well as the patient's age. During follow-up after ETV, late failure can occur and may lead to rapid deterioration. The aim of this report is to review the current data on the use of neuroendoscopy in children and to discuss the limitations and future perspectives regarding this procedure.

Title: Pediatric Obstructive Hydrocephalus: Comparative Outcomes of Endoscopic Third Ventriculostomy Alone Versus Single-Stage Endoscopic Third Ventriculostomy with Ventriculoperitoneal Shunt Placement
Snippet: Pediatric obstructive hydrocephalus is a major cause of morbidity in childhood and typically arises from conditions that block cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pathways, such as aqueductal stenosis, posterior fossa tumors, or fourth ventricular outlet obstruction [1,2]. Although ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placement has long been the conventional treatment, shuntrelated complications, including malfunction, infection, and frequent revision surgeries, remain significant challenges, particularly in the pediatric population [3,4]. Beyond the clinical burden, pediatric hydrocephalus also imposes a substantial long-term economic burden on families and healthcare systems, especially in resource-limited settings. 

Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) has emerged as a physiological alternative for non-communicating hydrocephalus by restoring CSF circulation. While ETV demonstrates high success rates in older children with aqueductal stenosis, its effectiveness in infants and in etiologically complex cases is variable due to differences in ventricular anatomy, cisternal development, and CSF absorption capacity [5,6,7]. In light of these limitations, some centers have adopted a single-stage strategy in which ETV is combined with VP shunt placement for selected high-risk pediatric patients. This approach may reduce early ETV failure by providing an immediate secondary CSF diversion route; however, concerns persist regarding the potential for unnecessary shunt implantation and the possibility of increased shunt-related complications [8]. Moreover, direct comparative studies between ETV alone and single-stage ETV with shunt placement remain limited, and optimal patient-selection criteria for the combined approach have yet to be established. 

The present study aims to compare the surgical outcomes, revision rates, and complication profiles of ETV alone versus single-stage ETV with VP shunt placement in pediatric obstructive hydrocephalus. We hypothesize that the combined approach may reduce early treatment failure in high-risk patients without significantly increasing infection rates or other shunt-related complications.
</snippet>

Title: Beyond shunt dependency: endoscopic third ventriculostomy in the contemporary management of paediatric hydrocephalus: a narrative literature review
Snippet: Hydrocephalus is a common neurosurgical condition in the paediatric population characterized by abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) within the ventricular system. It results from impaired CSF circulation, absorption, or excessive production and can lead to progressive ventricular dilation and increased intracranial pressure. Historically, ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunting has been the primary treatment modality; however, shunt systems are associated with high failure rates, infection, and lifelong dependency. Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) has emerged as an alternative surgical procedure that restores physiological CSF circulation by creating a stoma in the floor of the third ventricle, allowing CSF diversion into the basal cisterns. This narrative review aims to summarize the current literature regarding the indications, surgical technique, success predictors, outcomes, and complications of ETV in children. A comprehensive literature search was performed using PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar databases for studies published between 2000 and 2025. Keywords included “endoscopic third ventriculostomy,” “paediatric hydrocephalus,” and “ETV success score.” Studies involving paediatric patients (< 18 years) including cohort studies, clinical trials, and systematic reviews were included, while adult studies and case reports were excluded. Available evidence suggests that ETV is particularly effective in obstructive hydrocephalus, especially in cases of aqueductal stenosis and tumor-related obstruction. Reported success rates range between 50% and 80%, depending on patient age, aetiology, and prior shunt placement. The ETV Success Score has been widely adopted as a predictive tool for estimating procedural success. With advances in neuroendoscopic technology and improved patient selection, ETV has become an important treatment option in paediatric hydrocephalus. Future developments including ETV combined with choroid plexus cauterization and AI-assisted imaging may further enhance outcomes.
</snippet>

Title: Perioperative external ventricular drainage vs. no-EVD strategy in pediatric posterior fossa tumors—pilot study results
Snippet: Pediatric brain tumors occur within the posterior fossa in a relatively high percentage of more than one-half. Management of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulation disorders ranges from preoperative endoscopic third ventriculocisternostomy (ETV), implantation of an external ventricular drainage (EVD) pre-or intraoperatively, and delayed postoperative ETV and ventriculoperitoneal shunting (VPS) [2]. Incidence of preoperative and postoperative hydrocephalus is rarely reported. Literature rates for VPS implantation for persistent hydrocephalus range from 9 to 33.3% after posterior fossa surgery [2][3][4][5]. Some authors found that age at time of surgery, preoperative ventricular size measured as frontal and occipital horn ratio (FOHR), and implantation of an EVD are associated with the need of permanent CSF diversion [6][7][8]. Some authors advocate endoscopic third ventriculostomy prior resection [9]. For prediction of hydrocephalus outcome after posterior fossa tumor surgery, the modified Canadian Preoperative Prediction Rule for Hydrocephalus (mCPPRH) was proposed [10,11]. 

There is still an ongoing debate about the best treatment protocol: the use of preoperative EVD, treatment of hydrocephalus prior to tumor surgery with primary ETV, or a strategy of upfront tumor removal without any perioperative CSF diversion. 

The aim of the study was to analyze whether the use of EVD placement is superior to a no-EVD strategy in terms of hydrocephalus management and perioperative safety.

Title: Limitations of Neuroendoscopic Treatment for Pediatric Hydrocephalus and Considerations from Future Perspectives
Snippet: The cerebrospinal fluid (CsF) shunt has long been the classic treatment for pediatric hydrocephalus. it can resolve nearly all forms of hydrocephalus, regardless of the etiology. it is a simple procedure that can aid in having a relatively normal life. however, its failure rate is significant. The reported rate of shunt malfunction in the first year of placement is approximately 30%, and about 10% per year thereafter. The risk of infection is between 5% and 10%. in addition, the high rates of shunt complication such as slit ventricle syndrome are unacceptable by current standards. ][3][4][5][6][7][8] Therefore, the advent of neuroendoscopy was received with enthusiasm. Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) has been a routine surgical practice for the past two decades and provides an alternative to the CsF shunt. it is a straightforward procedure for diversion of the CsF and does not require placing devices in children's bodies. The utility and safety of ETV have been proven for obstructive hydrocephalus that occur secondary to aqueductal stenosis. however, for other indications, it is necessary to examine the anatomy and etiology, as well as the patient's age. During follow-up after ETV, late failure can occur and may lead to rapid deterioration. The aim of this report is to review the current data on the use of neuroendoscopy in children and to discuss the limitations and future perspectives regarding this procedure.

Title: Pediatric Obstructive Hydrocephalus: Comparative Outcomes of Endoscopic Third Ventriculostomy Alone Versus Single-Stage Endoscopic Third Ventriculostomy with Ventriculoperitoneal Shunt Placement
Snippet: Pediatric obstructive hydrocephalus is a major cause of morbidity in childhood and typically arises from conditions that block cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pathways, such as aqueductal stenosis, posterior fossa tumors, or fourth ventricular outlet obstruction [1,2]. Although ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placement has long been the conventional treatment, shuntrelated complications, including malfunction, infection, and frequent revision surgeries, remain significant challenges, particularly in the pediatric population [3,4]. Beyond the clinical burden, pediatric hydrocephalus also imposes a substantial long-term economic burden on families and healthcare systems, especially in resource-limited settings. 

Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) has emerged as a physiological alternative for non-communicating hydrocephalus by restoring CSF circulation. While ETV demonstrates high success rates in older children with aqueductal stenosis, its effectiveness in infants and in etiologically complex cases is variable due to differences in ventricular anatomy, cisternal development, and CSF absorption capacity [5,6,7]. In light of these limitations, some centers have adopted a single-stage strategy in which ETV is combined with VP shunt placement for selected high-risk pediatric patients. This approach may reduce early ETV failure by providing an immediate secondary CSF diversion route; however, concerns persist regarding the potential for unnecessary shunt implantation and the possibility of increased shunt-related complications [8]. Moreover, direct comparative studies between ETV alone and single-stage ETV with shunt placement remain limited, and optimal patient-selection criteria for the combined approach have yet to be established. 

The present study aims to compare the surgical outcomes, revision rates, and complication profiles of ETV alone versus single-stage ETV with VP shunt placement in pediatric obstructive hydrocephalus. We hypothesize that the combined approach may reduce early treatment failure in high-risk patients without significantly increasing infection rates or other shunt-related complications.

Title: Outcome of endoscopic third ventriculostomy in infants
Snippet: Hydrocephalus is a major cause of morbidity in the paediatric population, with an estimated prevalence of 1.2 in every 1000 children. In children, untreated hydrocephalus can have severe consequences including developmental problems, learning difficulties, and blindness. 1 Traditionally, shunts have been used as the main treatment strategy for hydrocephalus. More recently, endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) has emerged as a method of treatment for noncommunicating hydrocephalus (2) . ETV has been used on pediatric patients with aqueduct stenosis in many centers because of its advantage of providing a naturalflow route for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) within the range of indications. The long-term success rate has been reported to be as high as 80%, however, according to some reports on ETV, children younger than 6 months have a lower success rate of 12.5%. 3

Title: Beyond shunt dependency: endoscopic third ventriculostomy in the contemporary management of paediatric hydrocephalus: a narrative literature review
Snippet: Hydrocephalus is a common neurosurgical condition in the paediatric population characterized by abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) within the ventricular system. It results from impaired CSF circulation, absorption, or excessive production and can lead to progressive ventricular dilation and increased intracranial pressure. Historically, ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunting has been the primary treatment modality; however, shunt systems are associated with high failure rates, infection, and lifelong dependency. Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) has emerged as an alternative surgical procedure that restores physiological CSF circulation by creating a stoma in the floor of the third ventricle, allowing CSF diversion into the basal cisterns. This narrative review aims to summarize the current literature regarding the indications, surgical technique, success predictors, outcomes, and complications of ETV in children. A comprehensive literature search was performed using PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar databases for studies published between 2000 and 2025. Keywords included “endoscopic third ventriculostomy,” “paediatric hydrocephalus,” and “ETV success score.” Studies involving paediatric patients (< 18 years) including cohort studies, clinical trials, and systematic reviews were included, while adult studies and case reports were excluded. Available evidence suggests that ETV is particularly effective in obstructive hydrocephalus, especially in cases of aqueductal stenosis and tumor-related obstruction. Reported success rates range between 50% and 80%, depending on patient age, aetiology, and prior shunt placement. The ETV Success Score has been widely adopted as a predictive tool for estimating procedural success. With advances in neuroendoscopic technology and improved patient selection, ETV has become an important treatment option in paediatric hydrocephalus. Future developments including ETV combined with choroid plexus cauterization and AI-assisted imaging may further enhance outcomes.

Title: Perioperative external ventricular drainage vs. no-EVD strategy in pediatric posterior fossa tumors—pilot study results
Snippet: Pediatric brain tumors occur within the posterior fossa in a relatively high percentage of more than one-half. According to our own published data, 26% of all pediatric patients diagnosed with CNS tumor suffer from symptomatic hydrocephalus (HC) as presenting symptom (37 of 142 children) [1]. Management of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulation disorders ranges from preoperative endoscopic third ventriculocisternostomy (ETV), implantation of an external ventricular drainage (EVD) pre-or intraoperatively, and delayed postoperative ETV and ventriculoperitoneal shunting (VPS) [2]. We hypothesize that the combined approach may reduce early treatment failure in high-risk patients without significantly increasing infection rates or other shunt-related complications.

snippet.text: Hydrocephalus is a common neurosurgical condition in the paediatric population characterized by abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) within the ventricular system. It results from impaired CSF circulation, absorption, or excessive production and can lead to progressive ventricular dilation and increased intracranial pressure. Historically, ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunting has been the primary treatment modality; however, shunt systems are associated with high failure rates, infection, and lifelong dependency. Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) has emerged as an alternative surgical procedure that restores physiological CSF circulation by creating a stoma in the floor of the third ventricle, allowing CSF diversion into the basal cisterns. This narrative review aims to summarize the current literature regarding the indications, surgical technique, success predictors, outcomes, and complications of ETV in children. A comprehensive literature search was performed using PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar databases for studies published between 2000 and 2025. Keywords included “endoscopic third ventriculostomy,” “paediatric hydrocephalus,” and “ETV success score.” Studies involving paediatric patients (< 18 years) including cohort studies, clinical trials, and systematic reviews were included, while adult studies and case reports were excluded. Available evidence suggests that ETV is particularly effective in obstructive hydrocephalus, especially in cases of aqueductal stenosis and tumor-related obstruction. Reported success rates range between 50% and 80%, depending on patient age, aetiology, and prior shunt placement. The ETV Success Score has been widely adopted as a predictive tool for estimating procedural success. With advances in neuroendoscopic technology and improved patient selection, ETV has become an important treatment option in paediatric hydrocephalus. Future developments including ETV combined with choroid plexus cauterization and AI-assisted imaging may further enhance outcomes.
